fields.title: Two different metrics
fields.keyTakeaway: Latency is how long one user waits, throughput is how many users are served, and adding servers only fixes the latter.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: Users complain that the app is sluggish. The engineer replies that the system is handling the load. Who is right?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Both are right, and the conversation will not move forward until these two metrics are separated. Mixing them up leads to the team adding servers to solve a problem that does not change because of it, while the PM wonders why things did not get better.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: **[[latency|Latency]]** is how long a single request waits. Measured in milliseconds. This is what the user feels.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **[[throughput|Throughput]]** is how many requests the system processes per second. This is how many users it can handle.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: The metrics are related, but not the same. A system can process a thousand requests per second, each taking three seconds—throughput is great, but the user waits three seconds.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: *Low throughput*—more capacity, horizontal scaling, removing bottlenecks. Usually solved with money.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: *High latency*—reducing work per request: fewer database calls, caching, less data, fewer network hops. Almost never solved with money.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: Hence an important rule for the PM: **adding servers does not speed up an individual request.** It allows you to serve more requests with the same latency. If the complaint sounds like "opens slowly," servers will not help.
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: There is also feedback: under overload, latency grows because requests wait in a queue. This is the only case where adding capacity speeds up an individual request—and it looks like a latency problem, but is actually a throughput problem.
fields.sections/2/blocks/8/text: A chart helps tell them apart: if latency grows with load and drops during quiet times, it is throughput. If it stays the same around the clock, it is latency.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Two complaints analyzed using this framework.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: *"The main screen opens in three seconds."* The same day and night. Latency. Fixed by reducing the number of requests and materializing the rating—the topic covered in gate `DS2-G-A`. Servers would not have helped.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: *"Everything slows down on Monday mornings."* Only in the 9–11 window. Throughput: partner reports were eating up resources. Fixed by load segregation, not query optimization.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: Two similar complaints, two opposite solutions. Distinguishing between them took ten minutes of working with charts and saved a month of misdirected effort.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: In practice, problems get mixed up: a slow request under increasing load becomes even slower because it holds onto resources longer. You should still start troubleshooting by separating them.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Latency is how long one user waits, throughput is how many users are served, and adding servers only fixes the latter.
